newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols stay sensitive to dollar upticks.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols stay sensitive to dollar upticks.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options stayed sensitive to the spot market's upticks as the dollar briefly rose near last week's highs in U.S. trading, dealers said.
Even when the dollar was consolidating at lower levels earlier in the day, there was no aggressive selling in options, they added.

"We've definitely crossed the line into a different environment -- vastly different from last year, when as soon as we had spot pull back, vols immediately pulled back," said Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc.
"We've had enough (actual) volatility for a long enough period of time that it would take a pretty sustained period of inactivity to get vols hit significantly," he added.
Implied volatility for one-month dollar/mark was up at 10.3/10.5 percent from around 10 percent earlier in the day and 9.7/9.8 percent late on Friday.

Late in the U.S. morning, spot dollar/mark rallied nearly a pfennig from early lows, spurred by the dollar's strength against the Swiss franc. The franc dropped after reports that Swiss Finance Minister Kaspar Villiger had said he was "relieved" by the weak franc.
"I think a lot of it today had to do with spot," a trader at a U.S. bank said of the rebound in volatilities.
He noted that a somewhat reduced level of quote flows coming out of brokers' voice boxes compared with the past several days seemed to show a more passive attitude among option traders today.
In dollar/yen, volatilities were off slightly as spot stayed mostly in the mid-119 yen area in consolidative trading after hitting a 47-month high of 120.20 yen last Friday.
One-month implied volatility stood at 10.1/10.3 percent, about 0.3 point below late Friday levels but off early lows.
Traders noted that the dollar/yen volatility curve, which usually is in a fairly steep positive slope, has been flat or slightly inverted for several days.

They said the curve was likely to return to a positive slope soon unless volatilities continued expanding. Revercomb said the two- to three-month area could be the most vulnerable when the curve started to change shape.

"The long end is still going to have reasonable support from perception that we're in a new volatility environment," he said. "The short dates are going to whip back and forth as a function of what goes on over a few sessions."

Revercomb pointed out that while the trend was still for a higher dollar, the 120-yen level could start to weigh on the volatility market if the dollar starts to settle down at or below current levels, especially with a Group of Seven (G7) meeting scheduled on February 8 in Berlin.

"As we get closer to G7, it becomes planted in traders' minds that maybe some sort of lower-volatility interest is going to come out of the G7," he said. "That could start to cement 120 as more of a real top."
